1149.title: What the pandit reads
1149.hook: the pandit reads and argues, but has he understood
1149.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vichar, reflection on Gurbani, alongside reading it; study circles and katha, explanations of the hymns in the gurdwara, help listeners understand what is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Oankar traced Brahma, the mountains and the Vedas back to the One. Your line was from the one.

A book highlighted in yellow, page after page, the margins full of notes. Someone can quote chapter and verse, win every argument at the table, and still snap at the waiter five minutes later. Reading is one thing. Being changed by what you read is another. The Oankar knows this gap. It was answered, tradition says, to a pandit, a man who read and explained sacred texts, and the poem keeps turning to him with a simple question: you've read it, but have you understood?
screen: `PAGES HIGHLIGHTED IN YELLOW.` → `QUOTING ISN'T BEING CHANGED.` → `HAVE YOU UNDERSTOOD?`

segments.voice: The Oankar has a refrain, the line Sikhs call the rahao, the pause, where the poem stops to say what it's about. In paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles? Write the Name of the Lord, as the Gurmukh does. Notice the verb. Not stop writing. Write something else. The pandit is a man of the pen, and Nanak hands the pen back, pointed in a new direction. Elsewhere in the poem, in paraphrase: reading and reading, the pandit argues his case, but he doesn't know the treasure inside him. That's the gap from the hook: a person can master the words of a book and never meet the One the book is about. It would be easy to hear this as a story about someone else's priest. Sikh teaching doesn't leave it there. Guru Nanak says the same thing to every reader, and Sikh teachers turn it on their own reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Asa di Var he gives a striking picture. In paraphrase: you could read cartloads of books, whole caravans of them, through every month and every year of your life. Only one thing is counted; the rest is the noise of ego. The one thing is the Name, understood and lived. So the question isn't really for a pandit at a temple long ago. It's for anyone holding a book, or a phone, today. How much did I read is an easy question. What did it change is the hard one.
screen: `THE RAHAO: WHY WRITE THE TANGLES?` · `HE HANDS THE PEN BACK.` · `CARTLOADS OF BOOKS, ONE THING COUNTS.` · `WHAT DID IT CHANGE?` · then, large: `READ AND UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you've read lately, a verse, a sentence from a book, even one from this path, and say it to yourself slowly. Ask what it actually says, what it asks of you, and where it would make a difference, and stay with it until it feels less like information and more like something you know. If you pray, ask for understanding; if not, let the line settle.
What the pandit reads. In the Oankar, the reader who argues but hasn't met what's inside him; the refrain hands him the pen to write the Name. Today's word.
Your line: read and understand. Only one thing is counted. Go gently.

1150.title: The river bank
1150.hook: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time, says the Oankar
1150.howItsDone: Sikh hymns recall how short life is, as a reason to remember the Name now; the verses of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, are sung and read with the Gurus' hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pandit's reading: cartloads of books, and only one thing counted. Your line was read and understand.

A tree stands at the edge of a river. Its leaves are full, its shade is good, birds sit in it. From the path it looks like it will stand forever. But down at the waterline, where nobody looks, the current is working, a little soil every day. Then one ordinary afternoon, no storm, no warning, the bank lets go and the tree leans into the water. The Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, stops on that picture: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time.
screen: `A TREE AT THE WATER'S EDGE.` → `THE CURRENT WORKS UNSEEN.` → `ONE DAY THE BANK LETS GO.`

segments.voice: The Oankar walks through the letters, and at each one it sets down a teaching. Here the teaching is a picture: a tree standing on a riverbank, which can fall at any time. Notice what the picture doesn't say. It doesn't say the tree is weak, or foolish, or doing anything wrong. A tree on a riverbank is just where it is. The danger is in the ground under it, slowly being carried away. That's one way the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a human life: not as a disaster waiting to happen, but as something standing on ground that is always moving. The same picture shows up in the verses of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi poet whose words are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: a tree on the riverbank, how long can it keep its footing? How long can water stay in a pot of unbaked clay? Two voices from two different worlds, one image, kept side by side in the same scripture. So what is the picture for? Not fear. In the Oankar, the shortness of life becomes a question of timing. If the bank can give way any day, the things that matter can't wait for a safer season. The Name, the apology, the visit, the kindness you meant to get to: now is the bank you're standing on. In Sikh teaching, that's clarity, not gloom. The current is real. So is the shade, while it lasts.
screen: `A TREE THAT CAN FALL AT ANY TIME.` · `THE DANGER IS IN THE GROUND.` · `SHEIKH FARID: HOW LONG ITS FOOTING?` · `NOT FEAR: A QUESTION OF TIMING.` · then, large: `THE BANK GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Stand by water if you can, a river, a pond, even a running tap, or picture a riverbank under you, and let your attention go to your feet: the ground is taking your weight, holding today. Stay a few breaths with the water moving and the ground holding, then let one thing come to mind that you've been putting off for a safer season, and just name it. If you pray, remember the One beside the water; if not, let the water keep time.
The river bank. In the Oankar, a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time: life stands on moving ground, so what matters can't wait. Today's word.
Your line: the bank gives way. What matters can't wait for a safer season. See you on the path.

1151.title: The Gurmukh's learning
1151.hook: true learning is reflection on the Name
1151.howItsDone: Sikhs reflect on Gurbani through vichar: reading a hymn, hearing it explained in katha at the gurdwara, and thinking it over and discussing it with others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tree on the riverbank that can fall any day, so what matters can't wait. Your line was the bank gives way.

A cow lies in the shade long after she's finished eating, still chewing. Slowly, thoroughly, going over it again until it actually feeds her. Two days ago the Oankar asked the pandit whether he'd understood what he read. Today it answers its own question. If reading and arguing aren't the real thing, what is? The poem's answer has a name, and a person attached to it.
screen: `A COW, STILL CHEWING.` → `IF READING ISN'T IT,` → `WHAT IS REAL LEARNING?`

segments.voice: First, the person. The Gurmukh, as we've met all through these weeks, is the one whose face is turned toward the Guru. The opposite, in Gurbani, is the manmukh, the one turned toward their own mind. Both might own the same books. What differs is the direction. Now, the learning. In the Oankar, the Gurmukh's learning is vichar: reflection on the Name. It isn't skimming, and it isn't debating. It's going over a thing again and again, like the cow in the shade, until it feeds you. A pandit's learning, as the poem pictures it, ends in an argument won. A Gurmukh's learning ends somewhere else, and Guru Nanak says where in a hymn in Raga Asa. In paraphrase: when learning is reflected on, a person becomes a benefactor of others. That's a remarkable test for an education. Not how much you know, not how well you can defend it, but whether it has made you good for the people around you. Reflection, in this teaching, doesn't keep you in your head. It sends you out. Learning chewed long enough turns into kindness, patience, a hand offered. Some Sikhs practice this in an ordinary way: a line from the Guru Granth Sahib read in the morning, carried and thought over through the day, and talked about with others. The goal isn't to collect lines. It's to let one line work on you until it shows up in what you do.
screen: `GURMUKH: FACE TURNED TO THE GURU.` · `VICHAR: REFLECTION ON THE NAME.` · `LEARNING MAKES YOU GOOD FOR OTHERS.` · `ONE LINE, CHEWED SLOWLY.` · then, large: `REFLECT.`

segments.voice: Take one line, from the one, or the side that bows is the heavier, or any line that matters to you, and go over it the way the cow goes over her meal: once just hearing the words, once letting a single word stand out, once letting a face come to mind, someone this line could be good for. If your mind wanders, come back without fuss. If you pray, hold the line as a prayer; if not, let it simply be chewed.
The Gurmukh's learning. In the Oankar, real learning is vichar, reflection on the Name, and in Guru Nanak's Asa hymn, learning reflected on makes a person good for others. Today's word.
Your line: reflect. Slow, repeated, and pointed outward, like the cow in the shade. Be well.

1152.title: Writing on the forehead
1152.hook: a receipt in a coat pocket, a record no one else can read: the Oankar on what is written, and Japji on the deeds that write it
1152.howItsDone: In Sikh teaching, lekh, what is written, is spoken of alongside karam, deeds, and nadar, grace; some teachers present it less as fate to wait out than as a reason for honest work and seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gurmukh's learning: one line turned over until it feeds you. Your line was reflect.

A coat comes out of the closet after a long summer, and in the pocket there's a receipt: coffee for two, a date, a time. Faded, but still there. Nobody meant to keep it. It's a small record of something that actually happened. There's an old way of speaking about the record of a life: what's written on the forehead. The Oankar picks up that old picture of writing, and so does the Japji. Put the two side by side and a question comes up: who holds the pen?
screen: `A RECEIPT IN AN OLD COAT.` → `WHAT'S WRITTEN ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `WHO HOLDS THE PEN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Oankar. In one stanza, Guru Nanak speaks to a friend, sakhi, and says, in paraphrase: the writing does not get erased, the writing the Creator has written. What is written cannot be turned back; as it pleases You, so take care of it. The word for that writing is lekh. On its own, that could sound like a locked door: everything decided, nothing to do. But the same stanza ends, in paraphrase: by Your glance of grace, peace is found, reflecting on the Word. Grace is in the room. Now turn to the Japji. There Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: being called virtuous or sinful is not just talk. The actions you do, again and again, are written down, and you carry them with you. You sow, and you eat what you sow. Here the pen is in our own hand. Not one big deed, but karna, doing, repeated, until it becomes the record. So the scripture holds three things together: the Creator's writing, our own deeds writing day after day, and grace that can arrive. Sikh readers explain how these fit in more than one way, and this path won't settle it for them. But the picture is clear enough for a Tuesday. A record is being kept, and part of it is being written right now by what we actually do. Not by what we meant, or said we'd do. The receipt in the coat pocket was printed by a real afternoon.
screen: `THE WRITING IS NOT ERASED.` · `GRACE IS IN THE ROOM.` · `DEEDS, REPEATED, ARE WRITTEN DOWN.` · `PART OF IT IS WRITTEN TODAY.` · then, large: `WHAT'S WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who could use something small from you, a message, a ride, a meal, a thank-you, and pick one thing plain enough to finish before tonight. See yourself doing it, start to end, then rest with the breath. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out; if not, let the choice settle quietly, like ink drying.
Writing on the forehead. The lekh, the record of a life: in the Oankar, the Creator's writing; in the Japji, deeds done again and again, written down and carried. Today's word.

1153.title: Oankar close
1153.hook: a poem made of a scholar's own alphabet, sung back to him as an invitation: closing the Oankar with humble learning
1153.howItsDone: The Oankar is sung in kirtan and explained in katha, where a teacher goes through Gurbani line by line, seated before the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing on the forehead: the record a life writes, and the grace that can arrive. Your line was what's written.

Who explains things best? Often not the one who knows the most, but the one who remembers what it was like not to know: the patient older cousin, the coworker who says, I got this wrong for years, here's what finally helped. For a week this path has read the Oankar, Guru Nanak's long alphabet poem, spoken to a pandit, a teacher of letters. Today we close it, and the question isn't what the poem knows. It's how it teaches.
screen: `THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS NOT KNOWING.` → `A WEEK IN THE OANKAR.` → `NOT WHAT IT KNOWS. HOW IT TEACHES.`

segments.voice: First, look back. The poem opens with Oankar, the One, from whom even Brahma came. It asks whether the pandit has understood what he reads. It stands on a riverbank where a tree can fall at any time. It says true learning is reflection on the Name, and that a record is being written. Second, notice who it's spoken to. Its center line, the Rahao, says, in paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles? Write the Name of the Lord, as one who faces the Guru. Listen. It doesn't mock the teacher or tell him to burn his books. It leaves the letters on his board and asks them to carry the Name. That's an invitation, not a defeat. Third, look at how Guru Nanak speaks of himself. In the Japji, after a long list of the world's foolishness and cruelty, he signs the stanza, in paraphrase: lowly Nanak offers this reflection. The one bringing a new reading of the alphabet doesn't stand above the learner. He sits beside him and calls himself small. Fourth, put the two together. The Oankar teaches humility to the learned, and it teaches humbly. Knowledge that looks down on people has missed the poem's point. Knowledge that kneels beside someone and says, here, look at this letter with me, has caught it.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE OANKAR.` · `LISTEN, PANDIT: AN INVITATION.` · `LOWLY NANAK OFFERS THIS.` · `HUMILITY, TAUGHT HUMBLY.` · then, large: `HUMBLE LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you know well, a recipe, a tool, a song, a line of scripture, and one person who might want to learn it. Before planning what to say, remember the time you didn't know it, what confused you and what finally helped, and let your explanation start there, with one question you could ask them back. If you pray, say Waheguru once and rest.

Your line: humble learning. The best teacher sits beside you. The Oankar, closed.

1154.title: The tablet
1154.hook: the first thing anyone writes is a letter: Guru Nanak's Patti, a poem with one line of wisdom for each Gurmukhi letter
1154.howItsDone: In gurdwara Punjabi classes and at home, children learn the Gurmukhi letters, and teachers sometimes use the Patti to show that each letter can carry a line of the Guru's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Oankar, an alphabet that asks a teacher to listen. Your line was humble learning.

What was the first thing you ever wrote? Not a sentence. A letter. One shape, traced over and over, probably crooked. Before anyone writes a word, they learn the marks one at a time. Yesterday's poem sang the alphabet to a scholar. Today's takes it back to the beginner's desk. In Raga Asa, Guru Nanak has a poem named for the thing a child wrote on. Its name is Patti.
screen: `THE FIRST THING YOU EVER WROTE.` → `ONE SHAPE AT A TIME.` → `BACK TO THE BEGINNER'S DESK.`

segments.voice: Patti means a tablet, a writing board. Earlier on this path we heard the janamsakhi story of the boy Nanak at school, asking his teacher what the letters really point to. Today we open the poem itself. First, its shape. The Patti is an acrostic: each stanza opens with a letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet, and that letter starts a line about God and the soul. Letter by letter, the alphabet becomes a path. Second, how it begins. It opens with sasai, the letter S, and a line about the One who made the world, which we take up tomorrow. Then eevrri, in paraphrase: the Primal Being is the Giver, and that One alone is true. Then oorrai: praise the One whose limit no one has found. Three letters in, the poem has said who made things, who gives, and that the giver can't be measured. Third, why a tablet. A writing board is where learning starts small. You don't begin with a library. You begin with one mark, then the next. The Patti keeps that pace on purpose: one letter, and one line of wisdom to go with it. That's a way to learn anything deep: not all of it today, just the next letter. Fourth, the plain humility of the form. A writing board belongs to beginners, and the poem carries its name. The tablet stays a tablet. It just points further.

1155.title: Sasai: He made the world
1155.hook: a chair on a carpenter's bench: the Patti's first letter says the world was made, and its Maker is the one Master of all
1155.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of God as Karta Purakh, the Creator, and the Patti, sung in Raga Asa, opens with that thought on its first letter; the idea that one Creator made everyone is taught as a basis for equality and seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Patti, a tablet with a line of wisdom for each letter. Your line was letter by letter.

Sawdust on the floor, a half-built chair on the bench, and a carpenter running a thumb along a joint to feel whether it sits true. Nobody in that workshop would say the chair just happened. It's being made: measured, cut, fitted, on purpose. The Patti, the alphabet poem we opened yesterday, starts with a maker's word like that, and uses it for the whole world. Its first letter is sasai, the letter S.
screen: `A THUMBPRINT IN THE GLAZE.` → `SOMEBODY'S HAND WAS HERE.` → `THE PATTI'S FIRST LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the first stanza, in paraphrase: S. The One who fashioned the world is the one Master of all. Those whose minds stay fixed in that One's service, their coming into the world bears fruit. First, the word for made: saajee, fashioned, shaped, put together, the way a carpenter or a potter makes. The world, in this first letter, isn't an accident lying around. It's been put together on purpose. Second, one Master of all. Sabhnaa, of all of them. Not a master for the rich and another for the poor, not one for this village and another for the next. Some readers draw a quiet claim from that: if the same hand made everyone, nobody belongs to a different owner. Third, look what the stanza does next. It doesn't stop at admiring creation. It turns to the person reading: those who serve with their minds attached, their coming is safal, bearing fruit. The question shifts from who made the world to what you'll do in it. Fourth, why start here. A school slate could begin with anything. Guru Nanak's begins with the Maker, before anything else is learned, and every letter after is read in that light. The coffee cup, the sidewalk, the person in line ahead of you all fall under the same first letter.
screen: `SAAJEE: FASHIONED, LIKE A POTTER'S WORK.` · `ONE MASTER OF ALL.` · `SERVICE MAKES A LIFE BEAR FRUIT.` · `EVERY LETTER READ IN THIS LIGHT.` · then, large: `HE MADE IT.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one thing near you, a plant, your own hand, the sky through a window, and look at it as if it had been shaped on purpose: its edges, its color, how it holds together. Then look at the next thing the same way, with no need to explain anything. If you pray, say Waheguru, wonderful Lord, as you look; if not, let each thing be something someone could have made with care.
Sasai. The letter S, the Patti's first letter: the One who fashioned the world is the one Master of all, and serving that One makes a life bear fruit. Today's word.
